correctness.rationale: For fixed p>2 the exact beta-integral variance gives the affine reproducing kernel. The independent generalized-Gaussian/exponential representation yields a common radial factor converging in probability to one. Whenever normalized Euclidean length is bounded away from zero, all individual coefficients are negligible relative to their ell_2 norm, so the weighted triangular-array CLT and exact second moments justify convergence of absolute first moments to sqrt(2/pi). Small-norm rows are uniformly controlled by Cauchy-Schwarz. This proves the uniform Lebesgue profile and sharp norm. A strict-concavity defect for theta=2/p yields the necessity and sufficiency of p-mean flattening. Finite Monte Carlo evidence checks normalization but is not used to prove the infinite theorem.

originality.rationale: The claimed sharp coefficient, uniform full-ball Lebesgue profile, and necessity-and-sufficiency of normalized p-mean flatness were compared by implication against the inspected historical primary literature and relevant searchable research records. The 2005 independent-coordinate theorem supplies an input distribution but its Theorem 7 only has unspecified multiplicative constants, not this operator or sharp coefficient. The 2016 Euclidean-ball results address Sobolev errors for changing polynomial degree, not the present L-infinity norm at fixed degree as ambient dimension grows for finite p>2. Existing exact affine-projection formulae for ellipsoids, parallelepipeds, cross-polytopes, and the cube have different underlying domains and do not imply an exact continuum of finite p>2 norm constants or near-norming classifications. No equivalent statement was located. This is evidence of noncoverage, not a proof of absolute novelty.

value.rationale: The fixed-degree projection on uniform p-balls is a canonical least-squares approximation operator; identifying sharp sqrt(d)-growth and its gamma coefficient for each finite p>2 quantifies worst-case conditioning in high dimension. The uniform profile and complete iff near-maximizer rigidity show a nontrivial geometric effect: near worst-case evaluation points must be asymptotically flat, unlike the full spherical symmetry of p=2. This is a natural global classification rather than an arbitrary finite parameter case, and is not implied by the earlier up-to-constant moment bounds.
